Dear Hiring Team,

What sets me apart is the production engineering rigour I bring to AI, not demos. At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs at the core of a generative AI search platform on Vertex AI and Gemini. It was one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers, and I drove the decisions that make that kind of system safe to ship: model selection, retrieval quality, scaling patterns, and the guardrails a regulated bank requires before a generative system can go in front of a customer. Moving a generative system from demo to production takes a series of considered steps, evaluation, grounding, guardrails, observability, and that is where I have spent the last few years. They are the steps most teams underestimate.

Underpinning that, I have an engineering skill set across backend microservices, real-time event-driven architecture, and cloud-native API design. I architected Golang microservices and gRPC API contracts at ANZ, and before that designed and led delivery of a real-time, event-driven asset management platform at Macquarie, working directly with business stakeholders to translate operational processes into system design and cutting more than 50 hours of manual effort per week. I also build agentic workflows and AI automation across my own projects and not-for-profit work, designing, building, and shipping them end to end, which has changed how I think about what one engineer can deliver.

The client-facing side of this work is where my broader experience adds something. Earlier this year I ran an independent consulting engagement for Life Saving Victoria, defining the national scaling strategy for a mission-critical incident management platform and presenting it to executive leadership, accepted as the foundation for national adoption across seven jurisdictions. I am comfortable sitting with a client, breaking down the problem, and designing the system that solves it.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Fixed the typos in your Opus edit ("regulatory compliance", hyphenated "high-risk, high-impact"). Here's my read on propagation:

Your Macquarie change swapped the *quantified* "cut 50+ hours/week" for a *qualitative* "replacing high-risk, high-impact manual work with a digital solution that ensured regulatory compliance." That elevation fits **Opus** because the whole letter runs on regulated AI, guardrails, and compliance.

Where the old 50-hours metric still sits, my recommendation is **not** to propagate wholesale:

- **Real Time** (PM/commercial scaleup) — keep "cut 50+ hours a week." For a forward-deployed PM whose job is measurable adoption and NRR, the hard number is the stronger signal; "regulatory compliance" doesn't resonate with a startup audience.
- **Contour** (edtech SWE) — keep the metric, and more importantly keep the "working backward from what the business and users needed" hook (that's the product-first angle they screen for). Regulatory compliance is irrelevant to edtech.
- **KICK** (high-scale SWE) — already blends both: it has "regulatory traceability under load" *and* the 50-hours metric. Leave it; it's well-targeted.

So the new framing reads as appropriately Opus-specific. The one risk to weigh: "cut 50 hours" can undersell how high-stakes the Macquarie trading systems were, so if you'd rather lead with sophistication than efficiency everywhere, I can blend both into Real Time/Contour (e.g. "replaced high-risk manual work and cut 50+ hours a week").

content.text:
Compared the current Opus letter against the JD. Overall it aligns well on the heart of the role, with three gaps worth closing — one of them material.

**Strong alignment**
- *LLM-powered apps / GenAI in production* → para 1 (ANZ generative AI search platform, Vertex/Gemini, model selection, guardrails, grounding, observability). This is the core ask and you hit it hard.
- *Backend services, APIs, integration layers, reliable production* → para 2 (Golang microservices, gRPC, cloud-native API design, event-driven).
- *Translating business problems into AI solutions* → opener + para 2 + para 3.
- *Working directly with client stakeholders* → para 3 (independent consulting, client-facing, breaking down the problem).
- *Cloud (GCP/AWS)*, *4-5 yrs engineering*, *genuine interest in applied AI* → all covered.

**Gaps vs the JD's own language**
1. **Python — material.** "Python" is literally in the JD title (*LLM, GenAI, Python*) and "3-4 years of Python backend engineering is **required**." Your letter never says Python and leads on *Golang microservices and gRPC* — which actively spotlights the mismatch. A screener pattern-matching Python finds none and finds Go front-and-centre. This is the biggest misalignment.
2. **"RAG" not named.** The JD says RAG three times (it's a core deliverable). You describe RAG — "retrieval quality", "grounding", "AI-enabled search" — but never use the word. Naming it is a free, truthful alignment win (your ANZ search platform was retrieval-grounded generation).
3. **"Agentic" under-leveraged + measurable impact light.** It's a *Senior Agentic* role, and agentic only appears in the personal-projects clause. The letter also now carries few hard numbers, while the JD asks for "measurable impact."

**Recommended edits (truthful)**
- Work **Python** into the para-2 skillset line and soften the Go-only signal, e.g. "an engineering skill set across backend services in Python, Go, and Java, event-driven architecture, and cloud-native API design." Only if accurate to your depth.
- Name **RAG** once: "...the retrieval-grounded (RAG) search APIs..." or "...retrieval quality, grounding, and the RAG patterns behind it."
- Optionally lift **agentic** into the main narrative and restore one hard number for "measurable impact."

**Honest fit caveat:** edits help the letter *read* aligned, but the JD hard-requires 3-4 years of **Python backend** specifically. If your Python isn't at that depth (your CV has Go/Java as the deepest, Python in the toolkit), this is a genuine screen risk no cover letter fully closes — and per your own no-bluff rule, I won't claim Python depth you don't have. Worth deciding how hard to lean on Python before we finalise.

`needs input:` alignment is strong on GenAI/backend/client-facing; the real gaps are unnamed Python (hard-required, in the title) and unnamed RAG. Want me to (a) name RAG, (b) weave Python in at whatever depth is truthful, and (c) restore a measurable-impact number — and how hard do you want to play the Python angle given the 3-4yr requirement?

Dear Hiring Team,

I am an engineer who has worked across product, delivery, and stakeholder engagement. Through my own engagements I have built a far broader skill set than the title suggests, and I want to bring it into my next role with expanded scope. A forward-deployed role that sits inside the client's business and owns the commercial outcome is where that breadth pays off, and you are exactly the kind of team I want to do it with.

Every part of what this role needs, I have already done somewhere demanding. At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs on a generative AI platform, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank AI projects built to take AI directly to customers. I am fluent enough in API integrations, webhooks, and agent workflows to configure your product into a client's architecture myself, not hand it to someone else. At Macquarie I translated business requirements directly into a real-time platform, led the team that delivered it, and cut more than 50 hours of manual effort a week. Earlier this year I consulted independently for Life Saving Victoria, walking into a complex organisation with no playbook, breaking down the problem, designing the operating model and commercials, and presenting it to national executives as the foundation for national adoption. Alongside that I built and shipped a multi-tenant SaaS solo, replacing thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin a year, so I know what it takes to own something end to end and make it commercially real.

That combination, an engineer who can sit inside a client's stack, a builder who has shipped his own product, and an operator who can hold credibility with executives, is what makes a 30 to 60 day implementation sprint possible, and repeatable. I want to be in the accounts from day one, drive adoption, and feed what I learn back to the product.

My atypical background is exactly what turns a good delivery into a great one: the instinct to foresee the extra problem, solve it before it lands, and leave the client happier than they expected. I am a strong fit, and I would back myself in front of you to prove it. If we meet and you do not agree, that is fair. I do not think that is how it will go. The version where you take the chance ends with clients who are delighted with what we deliver, and me having grown into one of the best hires you made.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood

Dear Hiring Team,

Most senior engineers you talk to will understand your stack. Very few will also understand your domain from the inside. I do. I hold a Certificate IV in Training and Assessment, I have taught, and I have built training curriculum from scratch, designing how material is sequenced, where students get stuck, and what actually moves someone from confused to confident. When your product decisions come down to what genuinely helps a student learn, I am not guessing. That is the difference between building features and building the right features, and it is where I will deliver outsized value for Contour.

The engineering is senior and hands-on. At ANZ Plus I owned AI-enabled search APIs at the centre of a generative AI platform: Go microservices, gRPC, 80 percent plus test coverage on TDD standards I set for a 12-engineer team. At Macquarie I defined the architecture for a real-time platform and led a four-engineer team through delivery, cutting more than 50 hours of manual effort a week by working backward from what the business and its users actually needed before writing a line. I ship full-stack, most recently a multi-tenant SaaS I built and deployed solo on Next.js, Postgres, and Cloud Run, live with real users. I am comfortable across your stack and quick to pick up the parts of it I have not yet used in production.

I own features end to end, stay close to the student outcome, bring a point of view, push back when something does not make sense, and commit fully once a direction is set. I break large work into increments a team can review and deploy, and I write the tests and docs that genuinely help people ship, not gold-plating while students wait.

An engineer who can build at a senior level and also reason about pedagogy and the student journey is rare. For a company built on putting the student first, that combination is a real and direct advantage, and I would bring it to Contour from day one.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood

Dear Hiring Team,

Maintaining consistent low-latency chat, real-time viewer state, and platform stability across millions of concurrent sessions is a class of problem I have spent the last three years building for in production. At Macquarie I designed and led the delivery of a high-throughput, low-latency event-driven platform inside the trading and asset management division: event-sourced architecture on GCP, Kubernetes, and Pub/Sub, with full OpenTelemetry instrumentation and a four-engineer team to bring it across the line. The constraint was not just throughput, it was regulatory traceability under load, which means reliability and observability cannot be afterthoughts. That system replaced more than 50 hours of manual operational effort per week and passed architecture review. At ANZ Plus I moved into Golang microservices at bank scale: gRPC and Protobuf-first API contracts, Terraform-managed infrastructure, Kafka-backed event flows, and AI-enabled search APIs built to perform at the query volumes financial services infrastructure demands. I set and enforced an 80 percent test coverage standard and instrumented distributed tracing across the service mesh, because performance you cannot observe is performance you cannot trust.

Beyond the code, I bring the standards-setting and mentoring the role calls for. At Macquarie I defined the engineering standards the team adopted, TDD disciplines, coverage thresholds, code-review culture, and OpenTelemetry instrumentation patterns, and coached engineers through them. At Leidos I scaled an agile engineering organisation from two to six teams and defined the cross-team standards that held it together. These are how I have operated at senior level across every role, not soft skills tacked onto a technical resume.

KICK is at a genuine inflection point: a globally distributed real-time platform whose architecture has to evolve while it runs, migrating toward high-performance Golang services. That is precisely where a senior engineer who has built at this layer, understands what breaks under concurrency and load, and sets the standards a broader team can rally around makes the most difference. That is the role I am after and the environment in which I do my best work.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

What sets me apart is not only exploring the new opportunities AI opens up, but taking them into production, where cost, efficiency, and guardrails determine whether an AI solution genuinely meets the needs of the business. At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs at the core of a generative AI search platform on Vertex AI and Gemini. It was one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers, and I drove the decisions that make that kind of system safe to operate at scale: model selection, retrieval quality, scaling patterns, and the guardrails a regulated bank requires before a generative system can go in front of a customer. Taking a generative system into reliable production takes a series of considered steps, evaluation, grounding, guardrails, observability, and that is where my recent work has focused. They are the steps most teams underestimate. Alongside building generative AI, I also lean into AI-assisted development to improve my productivity, impact, and the value I deliver.

Underpinning that, I have an engineering skill set across backend microservices, real-time event-driven architecture, and cloud-native API design. I architected Golang microservices and gRPC API contracts at ANZ, and before that designed and led delivery of a real-time, event-driven asset management platform at Macquarie, working directly with business stakeholders to translate operational processes into system design, replacing manual, high-risk, high-impact work with a digital solution that ensured regulatory compliance. I also build agentic workflows and AI automation across my own projects and not-for-profit work, designing, building, and shipping them end to end, which has changed how I think about what one engineer can deliver.

The client-facing side of this work is where my broader experience adds something. Earlier this year I ran an independent consulting engagement for Life Saving Victoria, defining the national scaling strategy for a mission-critical incident management platform and presenting it to executive leadership, accepted as the foundation for national adoption across seven jurisdictions. I am comfortable sitting with a client, breaking down the problem, and designing the system that solves it.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

<result>Now let me do the startup files read as well -- actually I have everything I need. Let me produce the analysis.

---

## STRONG ALIGNMENT

- **Go fluency.** JD requires "fluent in... Go." Letter names "Go microservices, gRPC" at ANZ Plus directly. Strongest technical match.
- **Next.js + PostgreSQL.** JD core stack. Letter cites "multi-tenant SaaS I built and deployed solo on Next.js, Postgres, and Cloud Run." Concrete and solo-owned.
- **Test culture / coverage.** JD: "keep test coverage meaningful," Vitest/Jest. Letter: "80 percent plus test coverage on TDD standards I set for a 12-engineer team." The seniority of the standard-setting is well placed.
- **Product-first language.** JD: "Stay product first... not gold-plating while students wait." Letter mirrors this phrase almost exactly in para 3. This is not accidental overlap -- it reads as genuine alignment and the JD hiring team will notice the echo.
- **Meaningful increments.** JD: "Break large changes into reviewable, deployable steps." Letter: "I break large work into increments a team can review and deploy." Another tight match.
- **Push back then commit.** JD: "push back where it helps, and commit fully once a direction is set." Letter uses identical cadence. It lands.
- **Technical team leadership.** JD: "dependable technical presence the team can lean on." Letter: set TDD standards for 12-engineer team (ANZ), led 4-engineer team (Macquarie). This is the right evidence for that requirement.
- **Mission-alignment / domain.** JD explicitly values being "genuinely here for the mission of helping students." Letter's para 1 (Cert IV, teaching, curriculum design) is a rare and credible differentiator that no engineer without a training background can replicate. The framing is sharp.
- **Full-stack ownership.** JD: "build and deliver features across the stack." Letter: "I own features end to end." Consistent.
- **Fast-paced environment (bonus).** Implied via solo SaaS delivery and team-lead roles, though not explicitly claimed as startup experience.

---

## GAPS VS THE JD'S LANGUAGE -- ranked

1. **TypeScript not named.** This is the most glaring omission. TypeScript is listed first in "fluent in our core stack: TypeScript, Next.js, PostgreSQL, and Go." The letter names Next.js and Postgres but never says TypeScript. A hiring manager scanning for keyword hits will miss it entirely.

2. **Supabase not named.** The JD calls it out twice -- once in responsibilities ("Go services and Supabase edge functions") and once in requirements ("familiar with Supabase"). It's not a nice-to-have; it's in the day-to-day work description. The letter has no response to it.

3. **AWS not named.** JD: "familiar with... AWS services." Nick's profile explicitly includes AWS and Terraform at a senior level, but the letter only cites Cloud Run (GCP). The reader infers Nick's cloud experience is GCP-first, which is the wrong signal for this stack.

4. **SST / Pulumi (IaC) not named.** JD: "Help systems scale... with IaC (SST or Pulumi)." These are listed as responsibilities, not just nice-to-haves. The letter says "comfortable across your stack and quick to pick up the parts of it I have not yet used in production" -- which implicitly signals a gap without naming what the gap is. That hedge is weaker than no mention at all, because it draws attention to an unknown void.

5. **Prisma not named.** JD: "experience with ORMs (preferably Prisma)." Not mentioned. The solo SaaS uses Postgres but the ORM choice is invisible.

6. **Turborepo not named.** JD: "monorepo tooling like Turborepo." Technical breadth requirement. Not addressed.

7. **Vercel not named.** JD: "deploy via Vercel or similar pipelines." Cloud Run is not Vercel, and the letter doesn't bridge that.

8. **GitFlow / CI/CD / GitHub Actions not mentioned.** JD lists these under "Professional Standards" as explicit requirements. For a senior engineer at ANZ and Macquarie these are almost certainly real, but the letter leaves the box unchecked.

9. **On-call not addressed.** JD: "comfortable being on-call, and you take responsibility for the features you ship." Explicit requirement, zero coverage.

10. **PR/MR reviews not mentioned.** JD emphasises "thorough PR/MR reviews" as a core responsibility. The letter references tests and docs but not review culture, which matters for a team that will rely on Nick as a senior technical presence.

---

## GAPS VS THE JD'S LANGUAGE -- ranked

**1. "Net Retained Revenue (NRR)" -- completely absent.**
The JD names NRR as the commercial metric the role lives and dies by ("massive Net Retained Revenue (NRR)"). The letter never mentions it, and says "commercial outcome" twice where a precision phrase would signal you know what that outcome is. For a post-sale activation product this is the entire thesis.

The JD's whole opening three sentences explain what the company does ("continuous onboarding AI Agent that cures 'activation debt'"). The letter never names the problem space. "You are exactly the kind of team I want to do it with" is inert without naming what they do. A sentence naming the activation problem and why it's a hard PM problem would distinguish this letter from every other applicant who also read the word "forward deployed" and applied.

**3. "Proven experience in a B2B SaaS environment, ideally leading enterprise deployments, technical customer success, or solutions architecture."**
The letter's SaaS proof is AccessBuddy (pre-revenue, single volunteer tenant) and Macquarie (internal platform for an employer, not vendor-client SaaS). Neither is B2B SaaS deployment to a paying external enterprise. LSV consulting is the closest analogue -- walking into a client organisation and owning the implementation -- but the letter frames it as strategy/design, not a deployment or technical customer success engagement. The letter doesn't bridge this gap explicitly, and the JD marks it as "ideally" not a hard requirement, so there's room to argue transferability, but the argument isn't made.

**4. "Foundational functional leader, helping to define the blueprint for what 'great implementation' looks like."**
This is the upside the JD is offering and a signal about what the founders want: someone who will build the repeatable playbook, not just execute. The letter's single word "repeatable" in paragraph 3 skims the surface. Nick's LIMSOC work -- building the national scaling strategy and operating model from scratch with no prior template -- is precisely the proof for "define the blueprint," but it's framed in the letter as stakeholder engagement/exec presentation, not playbook construction.

**5. "Tier-1 companies (like Canva and Apollo)."**
The JD signals the calibre of current accounts. The letter never acknowledges the stakeholder environment -- nor does it demonstrate that Nick has operated at comparable account complexity. ANZ is a tier-1 financial institution with comparable scale; that brand value is sitting unused.

**6. The closer runs a risk for a founder audience.**
"If we meet and you do not agree, that is fair. I do not think that is how it will go. The version where you take the chance..." positions the hiring decision as them taking a chance, which frames the hire as a risk. For serial founders who just exited a company, the hire is a bet, but they want the candidate to reduce that perception, not invoke it. The directness is on-brand for Nick, but the specific framing could land as bravado rather than confidence.

**1. Name the commercial metric in the commercial paragraph.**
Replace "owns the commercial outcome" with a phrase that names NRR or post-sale activation specifically -- e.g., "owns the commercial metric that actually matters post-signature: whether the client activates, gets to value, and stays." This closes the NRR gap without overpromising.

**2. Open with one sentence naming the activation problem.**
The opener is generic (could apply to fifty roles). Add a single sentence that shows you know what the company does -- something like: "Activation debt is a real problem -- most B2B implementations stall somewhere between signed contract and realised value, and that gap destroys NRR faster than any churn event." Then pivot to why you're the person to close it. This names the problem, signals commercial literacy, and earns the reader's attention before paragraph 2.

You were, in effect, the forward-deployed technical PM. Own that framing.

**4. Add the LIMSOC "blueprint from scratch" claim explicitly.**

**5. Drop ANZ's project label and use the brand.**
"One of Australia's largest banks" or "ANZ" lands harder with a tier-1 account audience than "ANZ Plus... one of two initiatives across more than 100 bank AI projects." The tier-1 brand signals you have operated at enterprise scale that matches Canva and Apollo. Cut the internal programme framing.

**6. Soften the closer's framing of risk.**
Replace "The version where you take the chance ends with clients who are delighted" with something that makes the confidence land without invoking risk: "What you get is an engineer who already knows what great implementation looks like and is ready to build the template with you." Same confidence, no "chance" framing.

---

## HONEST FIT CAVEAT

The hard requirement Nick can't fully satisfy is **"proven experience in a B2B SaaS environment, ideally leading enterprise deployments, technical customer success, or solutions architecture."** Every piece of Nick's relevant experience was either internal (ANZ, Macquarie as employer, not vendor), solo-founded pre-revenue (AccessBuddy), or consulting to a public-sector volunteer organisation (LSV/LIMSOC). The letter can argue -- legitimately -- that his combination of consulting engagement delivery, technical depth, and SaaS founder experience is the functional equivalent, and the JD's "ideally" softens the requirement. But the argument must be explicit, because a hiring team that has already deployed into Canva and Apollo will notice the gap if it isn't addressed.</result>

- **Real-time, high-concurrency at scale.** The opener ("millions of concurrent sessions", "high-throughput, low-latency event-driven platform") maps directly to the JD's defining challenge ("4M+ concurrent viewers", "lightning fast chat messaging across massive global events"). This is the strongest thematic hit in the letter.
- **Golang microservices.** "At ANZ Plus I moved into Golang microservices at bank scale" names the primary language KICK is migrating toward. Go is the one of the three named minimum-qualification languages the letter satisfies.
- **Kafka.** Named explicitly at ANZ Plus -- sits directly in KICK's published tech stack.
- **Kubernetes.** Named at Macquarie ("GCP, Kubernetes, and Pub/Sub") -- K8s is in KICK's stack.
- **Terraform.** Named at ANZ Plus -- in KICK's stack.
- **Observability and distributed tracing.** OpenTelemetry at Macquarie ("full OpenTelemetry instrumentation"), "instrumented distributed tracing across the service mesh" at ANZ -- relevant to the Datadog-instrumented stack, though Datadog is not named (see Gaps).
- **Mentoring junior engineers.** Para 2 addresses this directly and with specific evidence: Macquarie (defined TDD standards, coverage thresholds, code-review culture, coached engineers through them), Leidos (scaled two to six teams, defined cross-team standards). No generic claim here -- it is backed.
- **Architecture and code quality.** "Designed and led the delivery"; "80 percent test coverage standard"; TDD; code-review culture -- maps to "architect and design scalable, high-performance software solutions" and "ensuring code quality, scalability, and maintainability."
- **Migration narrative.** Para 3 explicitly calls out "migrating toward high-performance Golang services" -- the exact phrase from the JD. Shows the candidate understands where KICK is in its trajectory.
- **Performance consciousness.** "Performance you cannot observe is performance you cannot trust" -- clear signal on the reliability-and-performance responsibility.
- **Preferred: large-scale product company.** Bank-scale at ANZ and a trading/asset-management division at Macquarie satisfy "Senior Software Engineer in a large-scale product company" (preferred qualification).
- **Stakeholder and team collaboration.** Leidos mention ("scaled an agile engineering organisation") plus standards-setting across teams addresses the collaboration responsibility.

## GAPS VS THE JD'S LANGUAGE -- ranked

**1. PHP (minimum qualification, named explicitly alongside Go and React)**
The JD states "Proficiency in multiple programming languages and frameworks relevant to the role (Go, PHP and React)." PHP is not mentioned once in the letter. KICK's current platform is PHP-based -- the team maintains PHP while building toward Go. This is the single largest gap: two of the three named minimum-proficiency languages (PHP and React) are absent from the letter, and Nick does not have PHP depth.

**2. React (minimum qualification, named alongside Go and PHP)**
React appears in the same minimum-qualification sentence as Go and PHP. The letter is entirely backend -- no frontend signal, no React mention, no acknowledgement of the "grow as a full-stack engineer" requirement the JD states explicitly. This reads as a backend-only candidate when the role explicitly wants full-stack appetite.

**3. AWS (primary cloud in the published tech stack)**
The perks section lists AWS first: "a vast cloud native tech stack including AWS, Microservices..." The letter opens with "GCP, Kubernetes, and Pub/Sub" at Macquarie, then stays GCP-aligned throughout. AWS is never mentioned. Nick is AWS certified and has AWS exposure -- this is a positioning failure, not a capability gap.

**4. "Identifying and resolving bottlenecks" (key responsibility, verbatim JD language)**
The JD explicitly names "optimise existing systems for performance, scalability, and reliability, identifying and resolving bottlenecks and inefficiencies" as a core responsibility. The letter signals the performance mindset ("performance you cannot observe is performance you cannot trust") but never demonstrates actually diagnosing or fixing a production bottleneck. No concrete example.

**5. Datadog (named in tech stack)**
KICK's stack explicitly includes Datadog. The letter has OpenTelemetry and distributed tracing -- the instrumentation layer -- but never names the observability platform. Hiring managers reading for stack fit may parse this as a Datadog gap even if the capability transfers.

**6. ArgoCD (named in tech stack)**
Not mentioned. GitOps and CD pipeline work is absent. If there is any delivery automation or pipeline work at ANZ or Macquarie, it belongs in the letter.

**7. Cloudflare (named in tech stack)**
Not mentioned. Nick operates Cloudflare on AccessBuddy and presumably understands CDN and DDoS mitigation at the application edge -- directly relevant to a globally distributed streaming platform. A single mention would close this.

**8. 6-7+ year floor**
Nick has approximately 6.5 years. He technically qualifies but sits at the very bottom of the stated range. The letter references "the last three years" of production work, which understates the full career and may inadvertently signal less experience than the threshold.

---

## RECOMMENDED EDITS -- truthful, specific

**AWS (high priority -- quick fix):**
Para 1 can absorb a brief clause. The ANZ sentence currently ends with "and AI-enabled search APIs built to perform at the query volumes financial services infrastructure demands." Add something factual before or after: Nick is AWS certified, and if any ANZ or adjacent infrastructure touched AWS, name it. Minimum repair: swap "GCP-centric infrastructure" for "cross-cloud infrastructure -- GCP at Macquarie, AWS-certified with hands-on exposure at ANZ" to eliminate the GCP-only read.

**Bottleneck resolution (high priority -- needs a real example):**
Para 1 or 2 needs one concrete incident: a Kafka consumer lag, a gRPC latency spike, a query plan that fell over under load. Even a single sentence -- "At ANZ, when [X bottleneck] emerged under [Y load], I [diagnosed with tracing] and resolved it by [Z]" -- directly answers the JD's most specific operational requirement. Do not use generic language here; the JD is precise, the answer must be too.

**Datadog:**
The observability sentence at ANZ could read: "instrumented distributed tracing across the service mesh, feeding into our Datadog observability pipeline" -- if that is accurate. If ANZ used a different tool (Dynatrace, New Relic, Splunk), name that instead; the signal is the same. If Datadog is truthfully accurate, name it.

**ArgoCD/GitOps:**
If ANZ used ArgoCD or any GitOps tooling (Flux, Helm releases driven from Git), add it. If not, the Terraform line can carry a gesture toward automated delivery: "Terraform-managed infrastructure with automated deployment pipelines" -- it is not ArgoCD but it signals the mindset without overclaiming.

**Cloudflare:**
Para 1 or 3 can absorb a single clause. The AccessBuddy context is accurate: "I run Cloudflare at the edge of my own live SaaS product" -- this is truthful and directly relevant to a global streaming platform that names Cloudflare in its stack.

**PHP -- the migration framing (cannot claim proficiency; can show awareness):**
Nick cannot claim PHP. What the letter can do is acknowledge the two-track reality more explicitly: "Maintaining velocity on an existing PHP codebase while incrementally migrating critical paths to Go is the exact kind of technical leadership this phase of KICK's platform requires." This shows the letter writer understands where KICK is today without fabricating a PHP credential. It also makes the migration framing in para 3 more specific and credible.

**React / full-stack appetite:**
A single line in para 3 answers this honestly: "My depth is in distributed backend systems; I am comfortable contributing across the stack and building toward the full-stack scope the role calls for." This is not a claim of React proficiency -- it is an honest signal on appetite, which is all the JD requires ("eagerness to grow as a full-stack engineer").

**Years anchoring:**
The opener could land "six and a half years building [X]" to pre-empt a screen against the 6-7+ threshold before the hiring manager calculates it from the resume.

**Scale anchoring:**
"Millions of concurrent sessions" is correct territory but imprecise against KICK's own published metric (4M+ concurrent). If Nick has any specific throughput numbers from Macquarie or ANZ (events per second, peak RPS, messages per minute on Kafka), replace the vague "millions" with a real number. Specificity always wins at this level.

---

## HONEST FIT CAVEAT

**PHP is a hard gap.** It is a stated minimum proficiency, KICK's letter lists it alongside Go and React, and the platform currently runs on PHP. No amount of letter framing closes a language gap. A hiring team that screens on the minimum-qualifications list will notice two of the three named languages are missing. The migration narrative (Go is where KICK is heading) softens this but does not eliminate it.

**React is a second hard gap in the same sentence.** The JD is not asking for a specialist -- it names React as one proficiency among several -- but the letter's total absence of any frontend or full-stack signal likely reads as a backend-only candidate. At KICK, where the Viewer Engagement team "ships user-facing features at scale," that matters.

**The combined PHP + React gap is structural.** The Go depth and the migration story are genuinely strong, and the rest of the tech-stack alignment (Kafka, K8s, Terraform, real-time at scale) is solid. But the minimum-qualification sentence lists three languages and the letter answers one. That is a genuine screen risk, not a framing problem.

**6.5 years at the floor of 6-7+:** Technically qualifies; practically thin. Not a blocker on its own but removes any buffer if other criteria are under-served.

**Honest bottom line:** This letter competes well on the Go-migration narrative, real-time scale experience, and mentoring/standards-setting. The AWS omission is a fixable positioning error. The PHP and React gaps are real and the letter cannot truthfully close them -- the best it can do is make the Go depth and migration rationale strong enough that a hiring manager chooses to overlook the language breadth gap.</result>

This is the strongest thematic hit in the letter.
- **Golang microservices.** "At ANZ Plus I moved into Golang microservices at bank scale" names the primary language KICK is migrating toward. Go is the one of the three named minimum-qualification languages the letter satisfies.
- **Kafka.** Named explicitly at ANZ Plus -- sits directly in KICK's published tech stack.
- **Kubernetes.** Named at Macquarie ("GCP, Kubernetes, and Pub/Sub") -- K8s is in KICK's stack.
- **Terraform.** Named at ANZ Plus -- in KICK's stack.
- **Observability and distributed tracing.** OpenTelemetry at Macquarie ("full OpenTelemetry instrumentation"), "instrumented distributed tracing across the service mesh" at ANZ -- relevant to the Datadog-instrumented stack, though Datadog is not named (see Gaps).
- **Mentoring junior engineers.** Para 2 addresses this directly and with specific evidence: Macquarie (defined TDD standards, coverage thresholds, code-review culture, coached engineers through them), Leidos (scaled two to six teams, defined cross-team standards). No generic claim here -- it is backed.
- **Architecture and code quality.** "Designed and led the delivery"; "80 percent test coverage standard"; TDD; code-review culture -- maps to "architect and design scalable, high-performance software solutions" and "ensuring code quality, scalability, and maintainability."
- **Migration narrative.** Para 3 explicitly calls out "migrating toward high-performance Golang services" -- the exact phrase from the JD. Shows the candidate understands where KICK is in its trajectory.
- **Performance consciousness.** "Performance you cannot observe is performance you cannot trust" -- clear signal on the reliability-and-performance responsibility.
- **Preferred: large-scale product company.** Bank-scale at ANZ and a trading/asset-management division at Macquarie satisfy "Senior Software Engineer in a large-scale product company" (preferred qualification).
- **Stakeholder and team collaboration.** Leidos mention ("scaled an agile engineering organisation") plus standards-setting across teams addresses the collaboration responsibility.

---

## GAPS VS THE JD'S LANGUAGE -- ranked

**1. PHP (minimum qualification, named explicitly alongside Go and React)**
The JD states "Proficiency in multiple programming languages and frameworks relevant to the role (Go, PHP and React)." PHP is not mentioned once in the letter. KICK's current platform is PHP-based -- the team maintains PHP while building toward Go. This is the single largest gap: two of the three named minimum-proficiency languages (PHP and React) are absent from the letter, and Nick does not have PHP depth.

**2. React (minimum qualification, named alongside Go and PHP)**
React appears in the same minimum-qualification sentence as Go and PHP. The letter is entirely backend -- no frontend signal, no React mention, no acknowledgement of the "grow as a full-stack engineer" requirement the JD states explicitly. This reads as a backend-only candidate when the role explicitly wants full-stack appetite.

**3. AWS (primary cloud in the published tech stack)**
The perks section lists AWS first: "a vast cloud native tech stack including AWS, Microservices..." The letter opens with "GCP, Kubernetes, and Pub/Sub" at Macquarie, then stays GCP-aligned throughout. AWS is never mentioned. Nick is AWS certified and has AWS exposure -- this is a positioning failure, not a capability gap.

**4. "Identifying and resolving bottlenecks" (key responsibility, verbatim JD language)**
The JD explicitly names "optimise existing systems for performance, scalability, and reliability, identifying and resolving bottlenecks and inefficiencies" as a core responsibility. The letter signals the performance mindset ("performance you cannot observe is performance you cannot trust") but never demonstrates actually diagnosing or fixing a production bottleneck. No concrete example.

**5. Datadog (named in tech stack)**
KICK's stack explicitly includes Datadog. The letter has OpenTelemetry and distributed tracing -- the instrumentation layer -- but never names the observability platform. Hiring managers reading for stack fit may parse this as a Datadog gap even if the capability transfers.

**6. ArgoCD (named in tech stack)**
Not mentioned. GitOps and CD pipeline work is absent. If there is any delivery automation or pipeline work at ANZ or Macquarie, it belongs in the letter.

**7. Cloudflare (named in tech stack)**
Not mentioned. Nick operates Cloudflare on AccessBuddy and presumably understands CDN and DDoS mitigation at the application edge -- directly relevant to a globally distributed streaming platform. A single mention would close this.

**8. 6-7+ year floor**
Nick has approximately 6.5 years. He technically qualifies but sits at the very bottom of the stated range. The letter references "the last three years" of production work, which understates the full career and may inadvertently signal less experience than the threshold.

---

## RECOMMENDED EDITS -- truthful, specific

**AWS (high priority -- quick fix):**
Para 1 can absorb a brief clause. The ANZ sentence currently ends with "and AI-enabled search APIs built to perform at the query volumes financial services infrastructure demands." Add something factual before or after: Nick is AWS certified, and if any ANZ or adjacent infrastructure touched AWS, name it. Minimum repair: swap "GCP-centric infrastructure" for "cross-cloud infrastructure -- GCP at Macquarie, AWS-certified with hands-on exposure at ANZ" to eliminate the GCP-only read.

**Bottleneck resolution (high priority -- needs a real example):**
Para 1 or 2 needs one concrete incident: a Kafka consumer lag, a gRPC latency spike, a query plan that fell over under load. Even a single sentence -- "At ANZ, when [X bottleneck] emerged under [Y load], I [diagnosed with tracing] and resolved it by [Z]" -- directly answers the JD's most specific operational requirement. Do not use generic language here; the JD is precise, the answer must be too.

**Datadog:**
The observability sentence at ANZ could read: "instrumented distributed tracing across the service mesh, feeding into our Datadog observability pipeline" -- if that is accurate. If ANZ used a different tool (Dynatrace, New Relic, Splunk), name that instead; the signal is the same. If Datadog is truthfully accurate, name it.

**ArgoCD/GitOps:**
If ANZ used ArgoCD or any GitOps tooling (Flux, Helm releases driven from Git), add it. If not, the Terraform line can carry a gesture toward automated delivery: "Terraform-managed infrastructure with automated deployment pipelines" -- it is not ArgoCD but it signals the mindset without overclaiming.

**Cloudflare:**
Para 1 or 3 can absorb a single clause. The AccessBuddy context is accurate: "I run Cloudflare at the edge of my own live SaaS product" -- this is truthful and directly relevant to a global streaming platform that names Cloudflare in its stack.

**PHP -- the migration framing (cannot claim proficiency; can show awareness):**
Nick cannot claim PHP. What the letter can do is acknowledge the two-track reality more explicitly: "Maintaining velocity on an existing PHP codebase while incrementally migrating critical paths to Go is the exact kind of technical leadership this phase of KICK's platform requires." This shows the letter writer understands where KICK is today without fabricating a PHP credential. It also makes the migration framing in para 3 more specific and credible.

**React / full-stack appetite:**
A single line in para 3 answers this honestly: "My depth is in distributed backend systems; I am comfortable contributing across the stack and building toward the full-stack scope the role calls for." This is not a claim of React proficiency -- it is an honest signal on appetite, which is all the JD requires ("eagerness to grow as a full-stack engineer").

**Years anchoring:**
The opener could land "six and a half years building [X]" to pre-empt a screen against the 6-7+ threshold before the hiring manager calculates it from the resume.

**Scale anchoring:**
"Millions of concurrent sessions" is correct territory but imprecise against KICK's own published metric (4M+ concurrent). If Nick has any specific throughput numbers from Macquarie or ANZ (events per second, peak RPS, messages per minute on Kafka), replace the vague "millions" with a real number. Specificity always wins at this level.

---

## HONEST FIT CAVEAT

**PHP is a hard gap.** It is a stated minimum proficiency, KICK's letter lists it alongside Go and React, and the platform currently runs on PHP. No amount of letter framing closes a language gap. A hiring team that screens on the minimum-qualifications list will notice two of the three named languages are missing. The migration narrative (Go is where KICK is heading) softens this but does not eliminate it.

**React is a second hard gap in the same sentence.** The JD is not asking for a specialist -- it names React as one proficiency among several -- but the letter's total absence of any frontend or full-stack signal likely reads as a backend-only candidate. At KICK, where the Viewer Engagement team "ships user-facing features at scale," that matters.

**The combined PHP + React gap is structural.** The Go depth and the migration story are genuinely strong, and the rest of the tech-stack alignment (Kafka, K8s, Terraform, real-time at scale) is solid. But the minimum-qualification sentence lists three languages and the letter answers one. That is a genuine screen risk, not a framing problem.

**6.5 years at the floor of 6-7+:** Technically qualifies; practically thin. Not a blocker on its own but removes any buffer if other criteria are under-served.

**Honest bottom line:** This letter competes well on the Go-migration narrative, real-time scale experience, and mentoring/standards-setting. The AWS omission is a fixable positioning error. The PHP and React gaps are real and the letter cannot truthfully close them -- the best it can do is make the Go depth and migration rationale strong enough that a hiring manager chooses to overlook the language breadth gap.</result>

content.text:
All five JD comparisons are in. Here's the consolidated read. I've ordered each role's gaps by what actually moves a screening decision, and flagged which fixes are truthful keyword/positioning wins vs. genuine fit limits. Several proposed fixes depend on facts only you can confirm (did you use Jira/Datadog/on-call/AWS hands-on?) — I've marked those rather than assert them.

## Cross-cutting theme
**AWS is under-named.** Contour and KICK both list AWS prominently; your letters signal GCP-only, yet you're AWS-certified. Naming AWS truthfully is a free win in both. Same pattern as the RAG/Python fix in Opus — the capability is there, the keyword isn't.

## Real Time — strong fit, but generic on *their* product
- **Strong:** API/webhook/agent-workflow configuration (near-verbatim), "30–60 day sprint", feedback-to-product, LSV ambiguity, commercial ownership.
- **Top gaps:** (1) **NRR** — the metric the role lives on — never named; (2) **"activation debt" / post-sale activation** — their whole thesis — not acknowledged, so the opener could fit fifty roles; (3) **LIMSOC as "blueprint from scratch"** under-sold (they want someone to *define* great implementation); (4) ANZ tier-1 brand sits unused.
- **Honest caveat:** you've never been *vendor-side* deploying SaaS into a paying enterprise (ANZ/Macquarie were internal; AccessBuddy pre-revenue; LSV public-sector). The JD softens this to "ideally", but the transferability argument needs to be explicit.
- *Note:* the analyst suggested softening your "take a chance" closer — I'd keep it, since you explicitly wanted that challenger energy. Your call.

## Contour — strongest technical + domain fit; keyword gaps
- **Strong:** Go, Next.js/Postgres, TDD/coverage, product-first echoes, the Cert IV/teaching domain differentiator.
- **Top gaps:** (1) **TypeScript not named** — it's first in their stack list, zero-cost truthful fix; (2) **AWS not named**; (3) **Supabase, SST/Pulumi, Prisma, Turborepo, Vercel** all unaddressed — and the current "quick to pick up parts I haven't used" hedge flags the void without naming it; (4) on-call, PR reviews, CI/CD if true.
- **Honest caveat:** Prisma/SST/Pulumi/Turborepo/Supabase are genuinely not in your history — their technical assessment will surface it regardless; best play is to name them with an honest Terraform/serverless bridge.

## Arcadian — AI-native fit is excellent; the must-have count is the risk
- **Strong:** delivery-confidence opener, dual-hat technical literacy, **AI-native (the sharpest edge — Claude partner callback)**, client data-flow line (near-verbatim), commercial acumen (near-verbatim).
- **Top gaps:** (1) **"3 custom web application builds"** is their *primary* screen — you name only one; (2) ticket-driven delivery from a BA + **UAT/release ownership** framed as engineer-fluency, not PM-ownership; (3) **multi-project management** silent; (4) stack vocabulary (Next.js/Nuxt) absent.
- **Honest caveat:** the 3-builds count is partly real, not just framing — AccessBuddy is clean, ANZ APIs are "platform" more than "web app", LifesaverOnCall is pre-launch. Name them and let them judge; don't overstate PM-delivery ownership. Also: "moving out of engineering" may read as a waypoint to a small agency — reframe to "I want to operate at this intersection."

## Thor — substance fits; PM-craft vocabulary missing
- **Strong:** AI in regulated FinTech, cross-functional leadership, dual-register comms (their exact ask), roadmap/exec, full lifecycle.
- **Top gaps:** (2) **Agile sprint/standup/backlog ownership** (Scrum Master is buried in a list); (3) **user research / voice-of-customer** silent; (4) **analytics-driven prioritisation** silent; (5) **requirements→user stories** (your Macquarie BA work is the proof, absent); (6) roadmap tool (Jira) unnamed.
- **Honest caveat (gap #1):** no formal **PM title** for any duration — a title/keyword screen catches it. Conscious apply-on-substance decision, which you've already made.

## KICK — Go/scale story is genuinely strong; language breadth is the wall
- **Strong:** real-time high-concurrency, Go, Kafka, K8s, Terraform, observability, mentoring (well-backed), the migration narrative (their exact phrase).
- **Top gaps:** (1) **PHP** — named minimum qualification, you don't have it; (2) **React / full-stack appetite** — absent (same min-qual sentence); (3) **AWS** not named (their stack lists it first); (4) no concrete **bottleneck-resolution** example; (5) Datadog/Cloudflare if true (you run Cloudflare on AccessBuddy — truthful add).
- **Honest caveat:** PHP + React is a *structural* gap — the JD names three languages, the letter answers one. Real screen risk; the best the letter can do is make the Go-migration rationale compelling enough to overlook it.

---

**What I'd action now (all truthful, low-risk):** name TypeScript + AWS (Contour), name AWS + Cloudflare + 6.5-years anchor (KICK), name the activation-debt/NRR problem and the LIMSOC-blueprint angle (Real Time), name the three builds + reframe the closer (Arcadian), surface the Macquarie BA/requirements work + Agile specifics (Thor).

**What I need you to confirm before I write them** (so I don't fabricate): did you use **Jira** (Thor/Arcadian), **Datadog or another APM** (KICK), **on-call** (Contour/KICK), and have **hands-on AWS** beyond the cert (Contour/KICK)? Tell me which are true and I'll thread only those.

################ 2 - Real Time - Forward Deployed Technical PM ################
Dear Hiring Team,

I am an engineer who has worked across product, delivery, and stakeholder engagement. Through my own engagements I have built a far broader skill set than the title suggests, and I want to bring it into my next role with expanded scope. A forward-deployed role that sits inside the client's business and owns the commercial outcome is where that breadth pays off, and you are exactly the kind of team I want to do it with.

Every part of what this role needs, I have already done somewhere demanding. At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs on a generative AI platform, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank AI projects built to take AI directly to customers. I am fluent enough in API integrations, webhooks, and agent workflows to configure your product into a client's architecture myself, not hand it to someone else. At Macquarie I translated business requirements directly into a real-time platform, led the team that delivered it, and replaced manual operational processes with a digital solution that laid the foundation for far greater efficiency. Earlier this year I consulted independently for Life Saving Victoria, walking into a complex organisation with no playbook, breaking down the problem, designing the operating model and commercials, and presenting it to national executives as the foundation for national adoption. Alongside that I built and shipped a multi-tenant SaaS solo, replacing thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin a year, so I know what it takes to own something end to end and make it commercially real.

That combination, an engineer who can sit inside a client's stack, a builder who has shipped his own product, and an operator who can hold credibility with executives, is what makes a 30 to 60 day implementation sprint possible, and repeatable. I want to be in the accounts from day one, drive adoption, and feed what I learn back to the product.

My atypical background is exactly what turns a good delivery into a great one: the instinct to foresee the extra problem, solve it before it lands, and leave the client happier than they expected. I am a strong fit, and I would back myself in front of you to prove it. If we meet and you do not agree, that is fair. I do not think that is how it will go. The version where you take the chance ends with clients who are delighted with what we deliver, and me having grown into one of the best hires you made.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com


################ 3 - Contour Education - Senior Software Engineer ################
Dear Hiring Team,

Most senior engineers you talk to will understand your stack. Very few will also understand your domain from the inside. I do. I hold a Certificate IV in Training and Assessment, I have taught, and I have built training curriculum from scratch, designing how material is sequenced, where students get stuck, and what actually moves someone from confused to confident. When your product decisions come down to what genuinely helps a student learn, I am not guessing. That is the difference between building features and building the right features, and it is where I will deliver outsized value for Contour.

The engineering is senior and hands-on. At ANZ Plus I owned AI-enabled search APIs at the centre of a generative AI platform: Go microservices, gRPC, 80 percent plus test coverage on TDD standards I set for a 12-engineer team. At Macquarie I defined the architecture for a real-time platform and led a four-engineer team through delivery, working backward from what the business and its users actually needed before writing a line and replacing manual processes with a solution that laid the foundation for far greater efficiency. I ship full-stack, most recently a multi-tenant SaaS I built and deployed solo on Next.js, Postgres, and Cloud Run, live with real users. I am comfortable across your stack and quick to pick up the parts of it I have not yet used in production.

I own features end to end, stay close to the student outcome, bring a point of view, push back when something does not make sense, and commit fully once a direction is set. I break large work into increments a team can review and deploy, and I write the tests and docs that genuinely help people ship, not gold-plating while students wait.

An engineer who can build at a senior level and also reason about pedagogy and the student journey is rare. For a company built on putting the student first, that combination is a real and direct advantage, and I would bring it to Contour from day one.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com


################ 4 - Arcadian Digital - Digital Project Manager ################
Dear Hiring Team,

You can hand me a custom build and not need to think about it again. It will get delivered, the client will stay confident, and you will not wait long to trust me with the next one. That is the bet I want you to make, and I am deliberately direct about it because I know how well I fit what Arcadian does.

The foundation is rare in one person. I have spent seven years as a software engineer, and across that time I have also worked as a solution architect, a Scrum Master, and a business analyst through dual-hat roles and secondments, so I understand a custom build from scoping through tickets to release from every seat at the table. At ANZ Plus I owned AI-enabled search APIs, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank AI projects built to take AI directly to customers, so I know what production-grade AI actually requires, not just what a demo shows. I use Claude every day, build my own agentic automation, and was on ANZ Plus's early Claude Code trial, which is the same ground Arcadian works on as a Claude partner.

On top of the engineering I bring real product experience. I directed a national platform strategy for a 199,000-member, $100M organisation, owning the operating model, roadmap, and commercials and presenting to the C-suite. I act as the de facto product manager for Life Saving Victoria's communications systems, and I built and shipped a multi-tenant SaaS solo, replacing thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin a year. I can sit with a client, map how their data moves between systems, and tell them honestly when something is worth building and when it is not.

I am at the point of making a deliberate move from pure engineering into delivery and product leadership, and this role is the logical next step. I know I am a strong fit. I am asking you to take the chance, and if you meet me and disagree, I will accept that. I am confident you will not.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com


################ 5 - Thor AI - Product Manager ################
Dear Hiring Team,

The hard part of AI in financial services is never the model, it is knowing which problem to aim it at and earning the trust of the engineers, data scientists, and compliance people who each see that problem differently. I have done it in production. At ANZ Plus I owned one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers. I set the product direction for our AI-enabled search platform, drove model selection, scaling, and guardrails in a regulated environment, and kept a 12-engineer cross-functional team aligned. I learned exactly what it takes to make generative AI safe and reliable enough to put in front of customers.

What I offer a company at your stage is range. In a small team the people who matter are the ones who can move across roles and lift whichever one needs lifting, and that is how I work. Across my career I have been a software engineer, a solution architect, a business analyst, and a Scrum Master, and alongside that I have run product and strategy: a national platform operating model and roadmap for a 199,000-member organisation, presented to national executives, and a multi-tenant SaaS I designed, built, and shipped solo that replaced thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin a year. I can talk architecture with your data scientists in the morning and translate the same work for a client's executive team in the afternoon, and I do not need a handover between the two.

ThorAI is solving a real problem: financial institutions with genuine AI ambition and a gap between what the technology can do and what they can bring to market. I understand that gap from inside a regulated bank, from the engineering bench, and from a strategy engagement that had to survive the jump from concept to executive sign-off. That is the work I want to be doing, and I would do it well here.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com


################ 6 - KICK - Senior Software Engineer ################
Dear Hiring Team,

Maintaining consistent low-latency chat, real-time viewer state, and platform stability across millions of concurrent sessions is a class of problem I have spent the last three years building for in production. At Macquarie I designed and led the delivery of a high-throughput, low-latency event-driven platform inside the trading and asset management division: event-sourced architecture on GCP, Kubernetes, and Pub/Sub, with full OpenTelemetry instrumentation and a four-engineer team to bring it across the line. The constraint was not just throughput, it was regulatory traceability under load, which means reliability and observability cannot be afterthoughts. That system replaced manual operational processes with a reliable digital platform that laid the foundation for far greater efficiency, and passed architecture review. At ANZ Plus I moved into Golang microservices at bank scale: gRPC and Protobuf-first API contracts, Terraform-managed infrastructure, Kafka-backed event flows, and AI-enabled search APIs built to perform at the query volumes financial services infrastructure demands. I set and enforced an 80 percent test coverage standard and instrumented distributed tracing across the service mesh, because performance you cannot observe is performance you cannot trust.

Beyond the code, I bring the standards-setting and mentoring the role calls for. At Macquarie I defined the engineering standards the team adopted, TDD disciplines, coverage thresholds, code-review culture, and OpenTelemetry instrumentation patterns, and coached engineers through them. At Leidos I scaled an agile engineering organisation from two to six teams and defined the cross-team standards that held it together. These are how I have operated at senior level across every role, not soft skills tacked onto a technical resume.

Most senior engineers you talk to will understand your stack. Very few will also understand your domain from the inside. I do. I hold a Certificate IV in Training and Assessment, I have taught, and I have built training curriculum from scratch, designing how material is sequenced, where students get stuck, and what actually moves someone from confused to confident. When your product decisions come down to what genuinely helps a student learn, I am not guessing. That is the difference between building features and building the right features, and it is where I will deliver outsized value for Contour.

The engineering is senior and hands-on. At ANZ Plus I owned AI-enabled search APIs at the centre of a generative AI platform: Go microservices, gRPC, 80 percent plus test coverage on TDD standards I set for a 12-engineer team. At Macquarie I defined the architecture for a real-time platform and led a four-engineer team through delivery, working backward from what the business and its users actually needed before writing a line and replacing manual processes with a solution that laid the foundation for far greater efficiency. I ship full-stack, most recently a multi-tenant SaaS I built and deployed solo on TypeScript, Next.js, Postgres, and Cloud Run, live with real users. My cloud and infrastructure depth runs across AWS, GCP, and Terraform; Supabase, SST, and Turborepo are not yet part of my production history, but they sit on ground I already know well, and I pick up tooling fast.

I own features end to end, stay close to the student outcome, bring a point of view, push back when something does not make sense, and commit fully once a direction is set. I break large work into increments a team can review and deploy, and I write the tests and docs that genuinely help people ship, not gold-plating while students wait.

An engineer who can build at a senior level and also reason about pedagogy and the student journey is rare. For a company built on putting the student first, that combination is a real and direct advantage, and I would bring it to Contour from day one.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

You can hand me a custom build and not need to think about it again. It will get delivered, the client will stay confident, and you will not wait long to trust me with the next one. That is the bet I want you to make, and I am deliberately direct about it because I know how well I fit what Arcadian does.

The foundation is rare in one person. I have spent seven years as a software engineer, and across that time I have also worked as a solution architect, a Scrum Master, and a business analyst through dual-hat roles and secondments, so I understand a custom build from scoping through tickets to release from every seat at the table. At ANZ Plus I owned AI-enabled search APIs, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank AI projects built to take AI directly to customers, so I know what production-grade AI actually requires, not just what a demo shows. I use Claude every day, build my own agentic automation, and was on ANZ Plus's early Claude Code trial, which is the same ground Arcadian works on as a Claude partner.

On top of the engineering I bring real product experience. I directed a national platform strategy for a 199,000-member, $100M organisation, owning the operating model, roadmap, and commercials and presenting to the C-suite. I act as the de facto product manager for Life Saving Victoria's communications systems, and I built and shipped a multi-tenant SaaS solo, replacing thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin a year. I can sit with a client, map how their data moves between systems, and tell them honestly when something is worth building and when it is not.

I am at the point of making a deliberate move from pure engineering into delivery and product leadership, and this role is the logical next step. I know I am a strong fit. I am asking you to take the chance, and if you meet me and disagree, I will accept that. I am confident you will not.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

The hard part of AI in financial services is never the model, it is knowing which problem to aim it at and earning the trust of the engineers, data scientists, and compliance people who each see that problem differently. I have done it in production. At ANZ Plus I owned one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers. I set the product direction for our AI-enabled search platform, drove model selection, scaling, and guardrails in a regulated environment, and kept a 12-engineer cross-functional team aligned. I learned exactly what it takes to make generative AI safe and reliable enough to put in front of customers.

What I offer a company at your stage is range. In a small team the people who matter are the ones who can move across roles and lift whichever one needs lifting, and that is how I work. Across my career I have been a software engineer, a solution architect, a business analyst, and a Scrum Master, and alongside that I have run product and strategy: a national platform operating model and roadmap for a 199,000-member organisation, presented to national executives, and a multi-tenant SaaS I designed, built, and shipped solo that replaced thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin a year. I can talk architecture with your data scientists in the morning and translate the same work for a client's executive team in the afternoon, and I do not need a handover between the two.

ThorAI is solving a real problem: financial institutions with genuine AI ambition and a gap between what the technology can do and what they can bring to market. I understand that gap from inside a regulated bank, from the engineering bench, and from a strategy engagement that had to survive the jump from concept to executive sign-off. That is the work I want to be doing, and I would do it well here.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

I am an engineer who has worked across product, delivery, and stakeholder engagement. Through my own engagements I have built a far broader skill set than the title suggests, and I want to bring it into my next role with expanded scope. A forward-deployed role that sits inside the client's business and owns the commercial outcome is where that breadth pays off, and you are exactly the kind of team I want to do it with.

Every part of what this role needs, I have already done somewhere demanding. At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs on a generative AI platform, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank AI projects built to take AI directly to customers. I am fluent enough in API integrations, webhooks, and agent workflows to configure your product into a client's architecture myself, not hand it to someone else. At Macquarie I translated business requirements directly into a real-time platform, led the team that delivered it, and replaced manual operational processes with a digital solution that laid the foundation for far greater efficiency. Earlier this year I consulted independently for Life Saving Victoria, walking into a complex organisation with no playbook, breaking down the problem, designing the operating model and commercials, and presenting it to national executives as the foundation for national adoption. Alongside that I built and shipped a multi-tenant SaaS solo, replacing thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin a year, so I know what it takes to own something end to end and make it commercially real.

That combination, an engineer who can sit inside a client's stack, a builder who has shipped his own product, and an operator who can hold credibility with executives, is what makes a 30 to 60 day implementation sprint possible, and repeatable. I want to be in the accounts from day one, drive adoption, and feed what I learn back to the product.

My atypical background is exactly what turns a good delivery into a great one: the instinct to foresee the extra problem, solve it before it lands, and leave the client happier than they expected. I am a strong fit, and I would back myself in front of you to prove it. If we meet and you do not agree, that is fair. I do not think that is how it will go. The version where you take the chance ends with clients who are delighted with what we deliver, and me having grown into one of the best hires you made.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

Maintaining consistent low-latency chat, real-time viewer state, and platform stability across millions of concurrent sessions is a class of problem I have spent the last three years building for in production. At Macquarie I designed and led the delivery of a high-throughput, low-latency event-driven platform inside the trading and asset management division: event-sourced architecture on GCP, Kubernetes, and Pub/Sub, with full OpenTelemetry instrumentation and a four-engineer team to bring it across the line. The constraint was not just throughput, it was regulatory traceability under load, which means reliability and observability cannot be afterthoughts. That system replaced manual operational processes with a reliable digital platform that laid the foundation for far greater efficiency, and passed architecture review. At ANZ Plus I moved into Golang microservices at bank scale: gRPC and Protobuf-first API contracts, Terraform-managed infrastructure, Kafka-backed event flows, and AI-enabled search APIs built to perform at the query volumes financial services infrastructure demands. I set and enforced an 80 percent test coverage standard and instrumented distributed tracing across the service mesh, because performance you cannot observe is performance you cannot trust. My hands-on cloud experience spans AWS and GCP, built across delivery at Leidos, Macquarie, and ANZ.

Beyond the code, I bring the standards-setting and mentoring the role calls for. At Macquarie I defined the engineering standards the team adopted, TDD disciplines, coverage thresholds, code-review culture, and OpenTelemetry instrumentation patterns, and coached engineers through them. At Leidos I scaled an agile engineering organisation from two to six teams and defined the cross-team standards that held it together. These are how I have operated at senior level across every role, not soft skills tacked onto a technical resume.

KICK is at a genuine inflection point: a globally distributed real-time platform whose architecture has to evolve while it runs, migrating toward high-performance Golang services. Holding velocity on an existing codebase while migrating critical paths to Go is exactly the kind of leadership this phase needs, and I am comfortable contributing across the stack, including React on the front end, as the role grows. That is precisely where a senior engineer who has built at this layer, understands what breaks under concurrency and load, and sets the standards a broader team can rally around makes the most difference. That is the role I am after and the environment in which I do my best work.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood

Dear Hiring Team,

I am an engineer who has worked across product, delivery, and stakeholder engagement. Through my own engagements I have built a far broader skill set than the title suggests, and I want to bring it into my next role with expanded scope. A forward-deployed role that sits inside the client's business and owns the commercial outcome is where that breadth pays off, and you are exactly the kind of team I want to do it with. Activation debt, the gap between a signed contract and a client actually live and getting value, is where most B2B revenue quietly leaks, and closing it fast is what protects net retained revenue. That is the problem I want to own.

Every part of what this role needs, I have already done somewhere demanding. At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs on a generative AI platform, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank AI projects built to take AI directly to customers. I am fluent enough in API integrations, webhooks, and agent workflows to configure your product into a client's architecture myself, not hand it to someone else. At Macquarie I translated business requirements directly into a real-time platform, led the team that delivered it, and replaced manual operational processes with a digital solution that laid the foundation for far greater efficiency. Earlier this year I consulted independently for Life Saving Victoria, walking into a complex organisation with no playbook, breaking down the problem, designing the operating model and commercials, and presenting it to national executives as the foundation for national adoption. Alongside that I built and shipped a multi-tenant SaaS solo, replacing thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin a year, so I know what it takes to own something end to end and make it commercially real.

That combination, an engineer who can sit inside a client's stack, a builder who has shipped his own product, and an operator who can hold credibility with executives, is what makes a 30 to 60 day implementation sprint possible, and repeatable. I have built repeatable delivery before, not just run it: I redefined the delivery approach at Life Saving Victoria and at Surf Life Saving Australia, a $100M national body now rolling that approach out across the organisation, and as a dual-hat Scrum Master in Defence I scaled delivery from two teams to six, including offshore teams. I have done it in very different environments, a digital bank at Macquarie and an innovation space at ANZ Plus, so I adapt the playbook to the place rather than force one template. I read a business fast and I am a quick study, which is the heart of forward deployment: get inside the client's operation, understand how value is actually created, and configure the product to deliver it. I want to be in the accounts from day one, drive adoption, and feed what I learn back to the product.

My atypical background is exactly what turns a good delivery into a great one: the instinct to foresee the extra problem, solve it before it lands, and leave the client happier than they expected. I am a strong fit, and I would back myself in front of you to prove it. If we meet and you do not agree, that is fair. I do not think that is how it will go. The version where you take the chance ends with clients who are delighted with what we deliver, and me having grown into one of the best hires you made.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
