Dear Hiring Team,

Most senior engineers you talk to will understand your stack. Very few will also understand your domain from the inside. I do. I hold a Certificate IV in Training and Assessment, I have taught, and I have built training curriculum from scratch, designing how material is sequenced, where students get stuck, and what actually moves someone from confused to confident. When your product decisions come down to what genuinely helps a student learn, I am not guessing. That is the difference between building features and building the right features, and it is where I will deliver outsized value for Contour.

The engineering is senior and hands-on. At ANZ Plus I owned AI-enabled search APIs at the centre of a generative AI platform: Go microservices, gRPC, 80 percent plus test coverage on TDD standards I set for a 12-engineer team. At Macquarie I defined the architecture for a real-time platform and led a four-engineer team through delivery, working backward from what the business and its users actually needed before writing a line and replacing manual processes with a solution that laid the foundation for far greater efficiency. I ship full-stack, most recently a multi-tenant SaaS I built and deployed solo on TypeScript, Next.js, Postgres, and Cloud Run, live with real users. My cloud and infrastructure depth runs across AWS, GCP, and Terraform; Supabase, SST, and Turborepo are not yet part of my production history, but they sit on ground I already know well, and I pick up tooling fast.

I own features end to end, stay close to the student outcome, bring a point of view, push back when something does not make sense, and commit fully once a direction is set. I break large work into increments a team can review and deploy, and I write the tests and docs that genuinely help people ship, not gold-plating while students wait. I give thorough PR reviews, treat ownership of a feature as extending past the merge to how it behaves in production, and have carried on-call for the systems I shipped at Macquarie.

An engineer who can build at a senior level and also reason about pedagogy and the student journey is rare. For a company built on putting the student first, that combination is a real and direct advantage, and I would bring it to Contour from day one.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood

Dear Hiring Team,

Maintaining consistent low-latency chat, real-time viewer state, and platform stability across millions of concurrent sessions is a class of problem I have spent the last three years building for in production. At Macquarie I designed and led the delivery of a high-throughput, low-latency event-driven platform inside the trading and asset management division: event-sourced architecture on GCP, Kubernetes, and Pub/Sub, with full OpenTelemetry instrumentation and a four-engineer team to bring it across the line. The constraint was not just throughput, it was regulatory traceability under load, which means reliability and observability cannot be afterthoughts. That system replaced manual operational processes with a reliable digital platform that laid the foundation for far greater efficiency, and passed architecture review. At ANZ Plus I moved into Golang microservices at bank scale: gRPC and Protobuf-first API contracts, Terraform-managed infrastructure, Kafka-backed event flows, and AI-enabled search APIs built to perform at the query volumes financial services infrastructure demands. I set and enforced an 80 percent test coverage standard and instrumented distributed tracing across the service mesh, because performance you cannot observe is performance you cannot trust. When our Kafka topics were overwhelmed by the volume of events flowing through them, I diagnosed the bottleneck and fixed it at the source, optimising what we published rather than simply scaling the consumers. My hands-on cloud experience spans AWS and GCP across Leidos, Macquarie, and ANZ, and I am comfortable with cloud deployments and edge services such as Cloudflare.

Beyond the code, I bring the standards-setting and mentoring the role calls for. At Macquarie I defined the engineering standards the team adopted, TDD disciplines, coverage thresholds, code-review culture, and OpenTelemetry instrumentation patterns, and coached engineers through them. At Leidos I scaled an agile engineering organisation from two to six teams and defined the cross-team standards that held it together. These are how I have operated at senior level across every role, not soft skills tacked onto a technical resume.

KICK is at a genuine inflection point: a globally distributed real-time platform whose architecture has to evolve while it runs, migrating toward high-performance Golang services. Holding velocity on an existing codebase while migrating critical paths to Go is exactly the kind of leadership this phase needs, and I am comfortable contributing across the stack, including React on the front end, as the role grows. That is precisely where a senior engineer who has built at this layer, understands what breaks under concurrency and load, and sets the standards a broader team can rally around makes the most difference. That is the role I am after and the environment in which I do my best work.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

The hard part of AI in financial services is never the model, it is knowing which problem to aim it at and earning the trust of the engineers, data scientists, and compliance people who each see that problem differently. I have done it in production. At ANZ Plus I owned one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers. I set the product direction for our AI-enabled search platform, drove model selection, scaling, and guardrails in a regulated environment, and kept a 12-engineer cross-functional team aligned. I learned exactly what it takes to make generative AI safe and reliable enough to put in front of customers.

What I offer a company at your stage is range. In a small team the people who matter are the ones who can move across roles and lift whichever one needs lifting, and that is how I work. I have lived in Jira for years, including as my team's champion for it, and I have designed, built, and shipped a SaaS product solo, concept to launch. I can talk architecture with your data scientists in the morning and translate the same work for a client's executive team in the afternoon, and I do not need a handover between the two.

I understand that gap from inside a regulated bank, from the engineering bench, and from a strategy engagement that had to survive the jump from concept to executive sign-off. That is the work I want to be doing, and I would do it well here.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood

1	Dear Hiring Team,
2	
3	What sets me apart is not only exploring the new opportunities AI opens up, but taking them into production, where cost, efficiency, and guardrails determine whether an AI solution genuinely meets the needs of the business. At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs at the core of a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) search platform on Vertex AI and Gemini. It was one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers, and I drove the decisions that make that kind of system safe to operate at scale. This included model selection, retrieval quality, scaling patterns, and the guardrails a regulated bank requires before a generative system can go in front of a customer. Taking an AI solution into reliable production takes a series of considered steps, evaluation, grounding, guardrails, observability, and that is where my recent work has focused. They are the steps most teams underestimate. Alongside building generative AI, I also lean into AI-assisted development to improve my productivity, impact, and the value I deliver.
4	
5	Underpinning that, I have an engineering skill set across backend services in Python, Go, and Java, real-time event-driven architecture, and cloud-native API design. I architected microservices and gRPC API contracts at ANZ, and before that designed and led delivery of a real-time, event-driven asset management platform at Macquarie, working directly with business stakeholders to translate operational processes into system design, replacing manual, high-risk, high-impact work with a digital solution that ensured regulatory compliance. I also build agentic workflows and AI automation across my own projects and not-for-profit work, shipping them end to end. One replaced thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin a year, and the experience changed how I think about what one engineer can deliver.
6	
7	The client-facing side of this work is where my broader experience adds something. Earlier this year I ran an independent consulting engagement for Life Saving Victoria, defining the national scaling strategy for a mission-critical incident management platform and presenting it to executive leadership, accepted as the foundation for national adoption across seven jurisdictions. I am comfortable sitting with a client, breaking down the problem, and designing the system that solves it.
8	
9	I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.
10	
11	Nicholas Wood

Dear Hiring Team,

I am an engineer who has worked across product, delivery, and stakeholder engagement. Through my own engagements I have built a far broader skill set than the title suggests, and I want to bring it into my next role with expanded scope. A forward-deployed role that sits inside the client's business and owns the commercial outcome is where that breadth pays off, and you are exactly the kind of team I want to do it with. Activation debt, the gap between a signed contract and a client actually live and getting value, is where most B2B revenue quietly leaks, and closing it fast is what protects net retained revenue. That is the problem I want to own.

Every part of this role I have already done somewhere demanding. At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs on a generative AI platform, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank projects built to take AI directly to customers, so I can configure API integrations, webhooks, and agent workflows into a client's architecture myself rather than hand it off. Earlier this year I consulted independently for Life Saving Victoria: I walked into a complex organisation with no playbook, broke down the problem, designed the operating model and commercials, and presented it to national executives as the foundation for national adoption. Alongside that I built and shipped a multi-tenant SaaS solo, from problem to live product, so I know what it takes to own something end to end and make it commercially real.

I build repeatable delivery, not just run it. I redefined the delivery approach at Life Saving Victoria and at Surf Life Saving Australia, a $100M national body now rolling that approach out across the organisation, and as a dual-hat Scrum Master in Defence I scaled delivery from two teams to six, including offshore teams. I have done it in very different environments, a digital bank at Macquarie and an innovation space at ANZ Plus, so I adapt the playbook to the place rather than force one template. I read a business fast, which is the heart of forward deployment: get inside the client's operation, understand how value is created, and configure the product to deliver it. That is what makes a 30 to 60 day implementation sprint not just possible but repeatable, and I want to be in the accounts from day one, driving adoption and feeding what I learn back to the product.

My atypical background is exactly what turns a good delivery into a great one: the instinct to foresee the extra problem, solve it before it lands, and leave the client happier than they expected. I am a strong fit, and I would back myself in front of you to prove it. If we meet and you do not agree, that is fair, but I do not think that is how it will go, and the version where you take the chance ends with delighted clients and me as one of your best hires.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

What sets me apart is not only exploring the new opportunities AI opens up, but taking them into production, where cost, efficiency, and guardrails determine whether an AI solution genuinely meets the needs of the business. At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs at the core of a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) search platform on Vertex AI and Gemini. It was one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers, and I drove the decisions that make that kind of system safe to operate at scale. This included model selection, retrieval quality, scaling patterns, and the guardrails a regulated bank requires before a generative system can go in front of a customer. Taking an AI solution into reliable production takes a series of considered steps, evaluation, grounding, guardrails, observability, and that is where my recent work has focused. They are the steps most teams underestimate. Alongside building generative AI, I also lean into AI-assisted development to improve my productivity, impact, and the value I deliver.

Underpinning that, I have an engineering skill set across backend services in Python, Go, and Java, real-time event-driven architecture, and cloud-native API design. I architected microservices and gRPC API contracts at ANZ, and before that designed and led delivery of a real-time, event-driven asset management platform at Macquarie, working directly with business stakeholders to translate operational processes into system design, replacing manual, high-risk, high-impact work with a digital solution that ensured regulatory compliance. I also build agentic workflows and AI automation across my own projects and not-for-profit work, shipping them end to end. One replaced thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin a year, and the experience changed how I think about what one engineer can deliver.

The client-facing side of this work is where my broader experience adds something. Earlier this year I ran an independent consulting engagement for Life Saving Victoria, defining the national scaling strategy for a mission-critical incident management platform and presenting it to executive leadership, accepted as the foundation for national adoption across seven jurisdictions. I am comfortable sitting with a client, breaking down the problem, and designing the system that solves it.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs at the core of a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) search platform on Vertex AI and Gemini. It was one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers, and I drove the decisions that make that kind of system safe to operate at scale. This included model selection, retrieval quality, scaling patterns, and the guardrails a regulated bank requires before a generative system can go in front of a customer. Taking an AI solution into reliable production takes a series of considered steps, evaluation, grounding, guardrails, observability, and that is where my recent work has focused. They are the steps most teams underestimate. Alongside building generative AI, I also lean into AI-assisted development to improve my productivity, impact, and the value I deliver.

Dear Hiring Team,

I am an engineer who has worked across product, delivery, and stakeholder engagement. Through my own engagements I have built a far broader skill set than the title suggests, and I want to bring it into my next role with expanded scope. A forward-deployed role that sits inside the client's business and owns the commercial outcome is where that breadth pays off, and you are exactly the kind of team I want to do it with. Activation debt, the gap between a signed contract and realised value, is where net retained revenue leaks, and closing it is the problem I want to own.

Every part of this role I have already done somewhere demanding. At ANZ Plus I owned the AI-enabled search APIs on a generative AI platform, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank projects built to take AI directly to customers, so I can configure API integrations, webhooks, and agent workflows into a client's architecture myself rather than hand it off. Earlier this year I consulted independently for Life Saving Victoria: I walked into a complex organisation with no playbook, broke down the problem, designed the operating model and commercials, and presented it to national executives as the foundation for national adoption. Alongside that I built and shipped a multi-tenant SaaS solo, from problem to live product, so I know what it takes to own something end to end and make it commercially real.

I build repeatable delivery, not just run it. I redefined the delivery approach at Life Saving Victoria and at Surf Life Saving Australia, a $100M national body now rolling that approach out across the organisation, and as a dual-hat Scrum Master in Defence I scaled delivery from two teams to six, including offshore teams. I have done it in very different environments, a digital bank at Macquarie and an innovation space at ANZ Plus, so I adapt the playbook to the place rather than force one template. I read a business fast, which is the heart of forward deployment: get inside the client's operation, understand how value is created, and configure the product to deliver it. That is what makes a 30 to 60 day implementation sprint not just possible but repeatable, and I want to be in the accounts from day one, driving adoption and feeding what I learn back to the product.

My atypical background is exactly what turns a good delivery into a great one: the instinct to foresee the extra problem, solve it before it lands, and leave the client happier than they expected. I am a strong fit, and I would back myself in front of you to prove it. If we meet and you do not agree, that is fair, but I do not think that is how it will go, and the version where you take the chance ends with delighted clients and me as one of your best hires.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

Most senior engineers you talk to will understand your stack. Very few will also understand your domain from the inside. I do. I hold a Certificate IV in Training and Assessment, I have taught, and I have built training curriculum from scratch, designing how material is sequenced, where students get stuck, and what actually moves someone from confused to confident. When your product decisions come down to what genuinely helps a student learn, I am not guessing. That is the difference between building features and building the right features, and it is where I will deliver outsized value for Contour.

The engineering is senior and hands-on. At ANZ Plus I owned AI-enabled search APIs at the centre of a generative AI platform: Go microservices, gRPC, 80 percent plus test coverage on TDD standards I set for a 12-engineer team. At Macquarie I defined the architecture for a real-time platform and led a four-engineer team through delivery, cutting more than 50 hours of manual effort a week by working backward from what the business and its users actually needed before writing a line. I ship full-stack, most recently a multi-tenant SaaS I built and deployed solo on TypeScript, Next.js, Postgres, and Cloud Run, live with real users. My cloud and infrastructure depth runs across AWS, GCP, and Terraform; Supabase, SST, and Turborepo are not yet part of my production history, but they sit on ground I already know well, and I pick up tooling fast.

I own features end to end, stay close to the student outcome, bring a point of view, push back when something does not make sense, and commit fully once a direction is set. I break large work into increments a team can review and deploy, and I write the tests and docs that genuinely help people ship, not gold-plating while students wait. I give thorough PR reviews, treat ownership of a feature as extending past the merge to how it behaves in production, and have carried on-call for the systems I shipped at Macquarie.

An engineer who can build at a senior level and also reason about pedagogy and the student journey is rare. For a company built on putting the student first, that combination is a real and direct advantage, and I would bring it to Contour from day one.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood

3	The hard part of AI in financial services is never the model, it is knowing which problem to aim it at and earning the trust of the engineers, data scientists, and compliance teams who each see that problem differently. 4	
5	What I offer a company at your stage is range. In a small team the people who matter are the ones who can move across roles and lift whichever one needs lifting, and that is how I work. That is the work I want to be doing, and I would do it well here.
8

3	Maintaining consistent low-latency chat, real-time viewer state, and platform stability across millions of concurrent sessions is a class of problem I have spent the last three years building for in production. At Macquarie I designed and led the delivery of a high-throughput, low-latency event-driven platform inside the trading and asset management division: event-sourced architecture on GCP, Kubernetes, and Pub/Sub, with full OpenTelemetry instrumentation and a four-engineer team to bring it across the line. The constraint was not just throughput, it was regulatory traceability under load, which means reliability and observability cannot be afterthoughts. I set and enforced an 80 percent test coverage standard and instrumented distributed tracing across the service mesh, because performance you cannot observe is performance you cannot trust. When our Kafka topics were overwhelmed by the volume of events flowing through them, I diagnosed the bottleneck and fixed it at the source, optimising what we published rather than simply scaling the consumers. My hands-on cloud experience spans AWS and GCP across Leidos, Macquarie, and ANZ, and I am comfortable with cloud deployments and edge services such as Cloudflare.

These are how I have operated at senior level across every role, not soft skills tacked onto a technical resume.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Dear Hiring Team,

Maintaining consistent low-latency chat, real-time viewer state, and platform stability across millions of concurrent sessions is a class of problem I have spent the last three years building for in production. At Macquarie I designed and led the delivery of a high-throughput, low-latency event-driven platform inside the trading and asset management division: event-sourced architecture on GCP, Kubernetes, and Pub/Sub, with full OpenTelemetry instrumentation and a four-engineer team to bring it across the line. The constraint was not just throughput, it was regulatory traceability under load, which means reliability and observability cannot be afterthoughts. That system replaced more than 50 hours of manual operational effort per week and passed architecture review. At ANZ Plus I moved into Golang microservices at bank scale: gRPC and Protobuf-first API contracts, Terraform-managed infrastructure, Kafka-backed event flows, and AI-enabled search APIs built to perform at the query volumes financial services infrastructure demands. I set and enforced an 80 percent test coverage standard and instrumented distributed tracing across the service mesh, because performance you cannot observe is performance you cannot trust. When our Kafka topics were overwhelmed by the volume of events flowing through them, I diagnosed the bottleneck and fixed it at the source, optimising what we published rather than simply scaling the consumers. My hands-on cloud experience spans AWS and GCP across Leidos, Macquarie, and ANZ, and I am comfortable with cloud deployments and edge services such as Cloudflare.

Beyond the code, I bring the standards-setting and mentoring the role calls for. At Macquarie I defined the engineering standards the team adopted, TDD disciplines, coverage thresholds, code-review culture, and OpenTelemetry instrumentation patterns, and coached engineers through them. At Leidos I scaled an agile engineering organisation from two to six teams and defined the cross-team standards that held it together. These are how I have operated at senior level across every role, not soft skills tacked onto a technical resume.

KICK is at a genuine inflection point: a globally distributed real-time platform whose architecture has to evolve while it runs, migrating toward high-performance Golang services. Holding velocity on an existing codebase while migrating critical paths to Go is exactly the kind of leadership this phase needs, and I am comfortable contributing across the stack, including React on the front end, as the role grows. That is precisely where a senior engineer who has built at this layer, understands what breaks under concurrency and load, and sets the standards a broader team can rally around makes the most difference. That is the role I am after and the environment in which I do my best work.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

The hard part of AI in financial services is never the model, it is knowing which problem to aim it at and earning the trust of the engineers, data scientists, and compliance teams who each see that problem differently. I have done it in production. At ANZ Plus I owned one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers. I set the product direction for our AI-enabled search platform, drove model selection, scaling, and guardrails in a regulated environment, and kept a 12-engineer cross-functional team aligned. I learned exactly what it takes to make generative AI safe and reliable enough to put in front of customers.

What I offer a company at your stage is range. In a small team the people who matter are the ones who can move across roles and lift whichever one needs lifting, and that is how I work. I have done the product manager's job in all but title: at Life Saving Victoria I owned the product vision, operating model, and roadmap for a national platform. I grounded it in research with the frontline lifesavers who use the system, carried their needs back as the voice of the user, prioritised the backlog around the highest-impact problems, and presented the result to national executives. As a dual-hat Scrum Master I have run sprints, stand-ups, and backlog prioritisation, and on a business-analyst secondment at Macquarie I turned stakeholder requirements into the specifications engineers built from. I have lived in Jira for years, including as my team's champion for it, and I have designed, built, and shipped a SaaS product solo, concept to launch. I can talk architecture with your data scientists in the morning and translate the same work for a client's executive team in the afternoon, and I do not need a handover between the two.

ThorAI is solving a real problem: financial institutions with genuine AI ambition and a gap between what the technology can do and what they can bring to market. I understand that gap from inside a regulated bank, from the engineering bench, and from a strategy engagement that had to survive the jump from concept to executive sign-off. That is the work I want to be doing, and I would do it well here.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood

Dear Hiring Team,

Great custom software is rarely lost in the code. It is lost in the gap between what the client needs and what gets built, and closing that gap is what I do. You can hand me a custom build and not need to think about it again. It will get delivered, the client will have their expectations exceeded, and you will not wait long to trust me with the next one. That is the bet I want you to make, and I am deliberately direct about it because I know how well I fit what Arcadian does.

The foundation is rare in one person. I have spent seven years as a software engineer, and across that time I have also worked as a solution architect, a dual-hat Scrum Master, and, on a Macquarie secondment as a technical business analyst, the person breaking scoped requirements into tickets and coordinating developers through testing, UAT, and release. I understand a custom build from every seat at the table. At ANZ Plus I worked on AI-enabled search APIs, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank AI projects built to take AI directly to customers, so I know what production-grade AI actually requires, not just what a demo shows. I use Claude every day, build my own agentic automation, and was on ANZ Plus's early Claude Code trial, which is the same ground Arcadian works on as a Claude partner.

I have delivered custom web application builds end to end, including Asset Master at Macquarie, a customer-facing feature platform at ANZ Plus, and LIMSOC at Life Saving Victoria, with three further production go-lives across government and defence at Leidos, alongside my own products built and launched on Next.js, the same stack Arcadian builds on. On the product side I directed a national platform strategy for a 199,000-member, $100M organisation, owning the operating model, roadmap, and commercials and presenting to the C-suite, and I act as the de facto product manager for Life Saving Victoria's communications systems. Running engineering, Scrum Master duties, and the LIMSOC programme in parallel built the discipline to keep several builds moving at once, tracked in Jira, where I was my team's champion for it, and I pick up tools like ClickUp in a day. I can sit with a client, map how their data moves between systems, and tell them honestly when something is worth building and when it is not.

I am now looking for the next step in my career, a deliberate shift to expand my scope, expand my impact, and really focus on the people side of technology through engagement and delivery. I know I am a strong fit. I am asking you to take the chance, and if you meet me and disagree, I will accept that. I am confident you will not.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

The hard part of AI in financial services is never the model, it is knowing which problem to aim it at and earning the trust of the engineers, data scientists, and compliance teams who each see that problem differently. I have done it in production. At ANZ Plus I worked on one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers. I drove model selection, scaling, and guardrails for our AI-enabled search platform in a regulated environment, and kept a 12-engineer cross-functional team aligned. I learned exactly what it takes to make generative AI safe and reliable enough to put in front of customers.

What I offer a company at your stage is range. In a small team the people who matter are the ones who can move across roles and lift whichever one needs lifting, and that is how I work. I have done the product manager's job in all but title. At Life Saving Victoria I owned the product vision, operating model, and roadmap for a national platform. I grounded it in research with the frontline lifesavers who use the system, carried their needs back as the voice of the user, prioritised the backlog around the highest-impact problems, and presented the result to national executives. As a dual-hat Scrum Master I have run sprints, stand-ups, and backlog prioritisation, and on a business-analyst secondment at Macquarie I turned stakeholder requirements into the specifications engineers built from. I have lived in Jira for years, including as my team's champion for it, and I have designed, built, and shipped a SaaS product solo, concept to launch. I can talk architecture with your data scientists in the morning and translate the same work for a client's executive team in the afternoon, and I do not need a handover between the two.

ThorAI is solving a real problem, financial institutions with genuine AI ambition and a gap between what the technology can do and what they can bring to market. I understand that gap from inside a regulated bank, from the engineering bench, and from a strategy engagement that had to survive the jump from concept to executive sign-off. That is the work I want to be doing, and I would do it well here.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/nicholas-wood/.claude/skills/ResumeExport

## Customization

**Before executing, check for user customizations at:**
`~/.claude/PAI/USER/SKILLCUSTOMIZATIONS/ResumeExport/`

If this directory exists, load and apply any PREFERENCES.md (e.g. a different default template or OneDrive destination). Otherwise proceed with skill defaults.

## MANDATORY: Voice Notification (before any action)

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:31337/notify -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"message": "Running the ResumeExport skill to export the document to docx"}' > /dev/null 2>&1 &
```
Then output: `Running the **ResumeExport** skill to export <doc> to .docx...`

## What this does

Tool: `~/.claude/PAI/TOOLS/DocxExport/` (bun/TypeScript, no python-docx). It does **template surgery** — keeps Nick's real `.docx` as the style template, preserves every non-body part byte-for-byte, and regenerates only `word/document.xml` from markdown by cloning the template's exact property blocks. So formatting fidelity is a consequence of reusing the originals, not re-derived.

## Workflow

1. **Get the markdown.** If Nick supplies a `.md`, use it. To pull editable markdown from an existing doc: `bun src/extract.ts resume|coverletter <file.docx>`. Author resumes in the contract below (full annotated example: `templates/resume.md` and `~/Documents/workspace/docx-export-proofs/virgin-cv/virgin-cv-source.md`).

2. **Export:**
   ```bash
   cd ~/.claude/PAI/TOOLS/DocxExport
   bun src/export.ts resume      <input.md> <out.docx>
   bun src/export.ts coverletter <input.md> <out.docx>
   # --template <docx> to template from a specific original instead of the default
   ```
   Defaults: resume → the 2026-06-12 Eng CV template; cover letter → the latest letter template (both in `profiles/`).

3. **Deliver.** Never put `.md` in OneDrive — only the rendered `.docx`. Write straight to the destination:
   - OneDrive: `bun src/export.ts ... "$HOME/OneDrive/02_Career/Job_Applications/2026/<Company>/Cover Letter - Nicholas Wood.docx"` (verify with `rclone lsl`; force-push with `rclone copy` if a mount stalls — see [[gotcha-onedrive-rclone-push]]).
   - Mac review: **delete the old file first, then scp** (overwriting in place can leave Word holding a stale copy):
     ```bash
     ssh mac 'rm -f ~/Downloads/<name>.docx'
     scp -p <out.docx> "mac:/Users/nicholaswood/Downloads/<name>.docx"
     ssh mac 'ls -la ~/Downloads/<name>.docx'   # confirm a current timestamp
     ```

4. **Verify** (optional but expected for new templates): `bun src/render.ts <out.docx> out.html` → screenshot on the Mac with headless Chrome, compare to the source. Or `bun src/verify.ts <expected.docx> <out.docx>`. Regression: `bun src/selftest.ts` (24 checks).

## Markdown contract

Resume contract (full table in `~/.claude/PAI/TOOLS/DocxExport/README.md`): `# Name`; contact lines (`|`-split, emails/URLs auto-hyperlinked); plain summary paragraph; `## Section` = bold+underline header; `- **Label:** rest` skill bullets (bold-italic label, tab, italic content); `### Company` then `**Role | Dates**` two bold lines; plain intro; `- bullet`; `**Technology:** …`; `**Degree** - Institution`. Leadership and Independent Engagements descriptions/bullets auto-nest (left 284/568/1004) to match the source; Experience stays flat.

Cover-letter contract: just the letter text, paragraphs separated by blank lines; a single newline inside a paragraph = line break (sign-off); inline `**bold**`/`*italic*`. Leading spacers come from the template.

## Gotchas

- **Resume template = the Eng CV, not the Hybrid.** The Hybrid has a different structure and was the original "formatting is wrong" bug. The default `profiles/resume.template.docx` is the correct Eng/Virgin source.
- **Delete the Mac copy before re-pushing.** Re-scp over an open/stale file is the "it's not updating" symptom — `rm` first, then `scp`, then confirm timestamp.
- **docx-preview renders are approximate** — Symbol bullets show as □ and continuous section breaks render as page breaks. These are renderer artifacts, NOT defects; Word renders `•` and flows correctly. Judge the actual `.docx` in Word, not the preview image.
- **Word AppleScript docx→PDF hangs headless over SSH** — don't rely on it for verification.
- **The Mac sleeps intermittently** — `ssh mac` can time out; retry. The workspace `code/` and proof PNGs sync via git; `.docx` does not (gitignored), so scp it directly.
- Related memory: [[reference-docx-export-tool]].

echo '{"ts":"'$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)'","skill":"ResumeExport","input":"8_WORD_SUMMARY","status":"ok|error"}' >> ~/.claude/PAI/MEMORY/SKILLS/execution.jsonl

############### COVER LETTER (pdftotext) ###############
Dear Hiring Team,



The hardest part of custom delivery is not scoping the work, it is shipping it reliably, on time and to
spec, build after build. That is what I do. You can hand me a custom build and not need to think
about it again. It will get delivered, the client will have their expectations exceeded, and you will not
wait long to trust me with the next one. That is the bet I want you to make, and I am deliberately
direct about it because I think I would be a great fit for your team.

What I bring first is direction and delivery leadership. At Macquarie I set the direction for Asset
Master, a process optimisation platform that replaced manual operational work across trading and
asset management, and led the team that delivered it. At Life Saving Victoria I have led the
technology behind LIMSOC, a mission-critical incident management system used in real-time coastal
emergencies, where I defined the AI strategy and led the first AI feature delivery while keeping the
wider book of work moving, shipping the most features the platform has ever delivered ahead of a
summer season. At the same time I defined the strategy to scale it nationally across a 199,000-
member, $100M organisation, owning the operating model, roadmap, and commercials, presenting
them to the C-suite, and uplifting the product and development practices behind it. Earlier, at Leidos,
I led a delivery team as it scaled from two scrum teams to six and brought the final stage of a two-
year Department of Defence data discovery platform to go-live, turning months of analyst work into
seconds.

Running that much at once takes discipline. I keep several builds moving in parallel, tracked in Jira
where I was my team's champion, and I stay close enough to the commercial picture to sit with a
client, map how their data moves between systems, and tell them honestly when something is worth
building and when it is not. Underneath it all sits a real engineering foundation, seven years as a
software engineer alongside spells as a solution architect, a dual-hat Scrum Master, and a technical
business analyst breaking scoped requirements into tickets and coordinating developers through
testing, UAT, and release, so I understand a custom build from every seat at the table.

The AI side is where Arcadian and I line up most closely. At ANZ Plus I worked on AI-enabled search
APIs, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank AI projects built to take AI directly to
customers, so I know what production-grade AI actually requires, not just what a demo shows. I use
Claude every day, build my own agentic automation, and was on ANZ Plus's early Claude Code trial,
the same ground Arcadian works on as a Claude partner.

I am now looking for the next step in my career, a deliberate shift to expand my scope, expand my
impact, and really focus on the people side of technology through engagement and delivery. I know I
am a strong fit. I am asking you to take the chance, and if you meet me and disagree, I will accept
that. I am confident you will not.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.



Nicholas Wood

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Dear Hiring Team,

The hardest part of custom delivery is not scoping the work, it is shipping it reliably, on time and to spec, build after build. That is what I do. You can hand me a custom build and not need to think about it again. It will get delivered, the client will have their expectations exceeded, and you will not wait long to trust me with the next one. That is the bet I want you to make, and I am deliberately direct about it because I think I would be a great fit for your team.

What I bring first is direction and delivery leadership. At Macquarie I set the direction for Asset Master, a process optimisation platform that replaced manual operational work across trading and asset management, and led the team that delivered it. At Life Saving Victoria I have led the technology behind LIMSOC, a mission-critical incident management system used in real-time coastal emergencies, where I defined the AI strategy and led the first AI feature delivery while keeping the wider book of work moving, shipping the most features the platform has ever delivered ahead of a summer season. At the same time I defined the strategy to scale it nationally across a 199,000-member, $100M organisation, owning the operating model, roadmap, and commercials, presenting them to the C-suite, and uplifting the product and development practices behind it. Earlier, at Leidos, I led a delivery team as it scaled from two scrum teams to six and brought the final stage of a two-year Department of Defence data discovery platform to go-live, turning months of analyst work into seconds.

Running that much at once takes discipline. I keep several builds moving in parallel, tracked in Jira where I was my team's champion, and I stay close enough to the commercial picture to sit with a client, map how their data moves between systems, and tell them honestly when something is worth building and when it is not. Underneath it all sits a real engineering foundation, seven years as a software engineer alongside spells as a solution architect, a dual-hat Scrum Master, and a technical business analyst breaking scoped requirements into tickets and coordinating developers through testing, UAT, and release, so I understand a custom build from every seat at the table.

The AI side is where Arcadian and I line up most closely. At ANZ Plus I worked on AI-enabled search APIs, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank AI projects built to take AI directly to customers, so I know what production-grade AI actually requires, not just what a demo shows. I use Claude every day, build my own agentic automation, and was on ANZ Plus's early Claude Code trial, the same ground Arcadian works on as a Claude partner.

I am now looking for the next step in my career, a deliberate shift to expand my scope, expand my impact, and really focus on the people side of technology through engagement and delivery. I know I am a strong fit. I am asking you to take the chance, and if you meet me and disagree, I will accept that. I am confident you will not.

I look forward to the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com
